claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is governed by formation of a dual-layered bilayer core–shell structure.
The core–shell structure enhances yield stress in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
The core–shell structure enhances plasticity in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
The material starts as an as-cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy.
The proposed intervention applies heat treatments at 700, 900, and 1100 °C for different durations.
The comparison is to be performed under vacuum heat-treatment conditions.
Laser additive manufacturing or selective laser melting is part of the proposed processing conditions.
Formation of the core–shell structure improves interface bonding.
Formation of the core–shell structure reduces stress concentration.
Improved interface bonding and reduced stress concentration enhance mechanical properties.
Heat-treated alloys will have greater yield stress than the untreated as-cast baseline.
Heat-treated alloys will have greater plasticity than the untreated as-cast baseline.
The intervention will enhance high-temperature stability.
The intervention will enhance corrosion resistance.
The baseline is an as-cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy without heat treatment.
The hypothesis is restricted to the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy family and may not transfer to other alloy systems.
The mechanism of core–shell formation and its influence on properties is not fully understood.
Failure of heat treatment to improve both yield stress and plasticity relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial state and baseline are described as as-cast, while the conditions specify laser additive manufacturing and selective laser melting. These are distinct manufacturing routes, so the actual baseline and controlled processing history are ambiguous.

The main hypothesis concerns phase stability, but the falsification rule tests only yield stress and plasticity; it does not require measurement of phase stability or demonstration that a core–shell structure formed.
